title: How Computers Store Text - ASCII, Unicode, UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32
description:
How do computers store text? In this video you will learn how we encode text into numbers, and decode those back into text. We'll talk about the ASCII and Unicode standards, as well as the UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32 text encodings. The former standards represent characters and codepoints respectively to store text in binary. The UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32 encodings are used to actually represent Unicode codepoints. The video gives concrete examples of how this works.

title: Data Compression and Extracting Information | Six Minutes: AP Computer Science Principles, Part 15
description:
Six Minutes: AP Computer Science Principles, Part 15: Data Compression and Extracting Information: Lossy vs. lossless trade-offs, 2.2; then Extracting Information

Lossless compression restores the original data exactly, while lossy compression shrinks more but loses data permanently. Run-length encoding shows how lossless methods replace repeated values with counts. Then: Topic 2.3: turn a pile of data into an answer by filtering with a loop and IF, then spotting patterns and trends. title: Exercises: Number Limits, Overflow, and roundoff  (AP Computer Science Principles Unit 1)
description:
Today's video discusses the difference between overflow errors and roundoff errors. Essentially, they are the same phenomenon on opposite sides of the decimal point. A number that is too large to be represented results in an overflow error. A number that has too many digits AFTER the decimal point can result in a roundoff error.

You can find this exercise set here:
https://www.khanacademy.org/computing/ap-computer-science-principles/x2d2f703b37b450a3:digital-information/x2d2f703b37b450a3:number-limits-overflow-and-roundoff/e/number-limits--overflow--and-round-off

title: What Is User Interface (UI)?
description:
User interfaces (UIs) are what allow us to interact with and navigate through our favorite programs and devices. Every time you click a button on a website or swipe to a different screen, you're engaging with UI.

Having a good UI is critical to a technology's success. Most people wouldn't stick with an app or device if it were clumsy or awkward to use. That's why UI design is so important and often tied into UX (user experience).

In the video above, we'll dive deeper into UIs and UI design. You'll learn about some common examples of UIs, the difference between good and bad UIs, and how qualities like responsiveness and consistency play a role in keeping users happy.

title: Algorithmic Bias and Fairness: Crash Course AI #18
description:
Check out Jabril's collab with "Above the Noise" about Deepfakes: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ro8b69VeL9U
Today, we're going to talk about five common types of algorithmic bias we should pay attention to: data that reflects existing biases, unbalanced classes in training data, data that doesn't capture the right value, data that is amplified by feedback loops, and malicious data. Now bias itself isn't necessarily a terrible thing, our brains often use it to take shortcuts by finding patterns, but bias can become a problem if we don't acknowledge exceptions to patterns or if we allow it to discriminate.

title: AP CSP 3 18 1 Undecidable Problems
description: presented by Mrs. Julia Alano, introduces the concept of undecidable problems in computer science. The video clarifies the distinction between decidable problems, which always have a yes or no algorithmic solution for any input, and undecidable problems, where such a universal algorithm does not exist. A key example provided is the halting problem, which questions whether any given computer program with specific inputs will eventually stop or run indefinitely. The lesson emphasizes that for undecidable problems, no single algorithm can consistently determine a yes or no answer across all possible inputs.

title: The Halting Problem: The Unsolvable Problem
description:
One of the most influential problems and proofs in computer science, first introduced and proved impossible to solve by Alan Turing. The video provides the idea of this incredibly clever proof. I highly recommend anyone who is comfortable with mathematical proofs to read the formal proof to the problem (look at additional resources below for information).

Also, the video does not cover this, but the significance of this unsolvable problem cannot be understated.
